questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: Term behaviour read off the leading powers
questions.learningObjective: Determine the behaviour of a series from the leading powers of its terms.
questions.stem: Glossary entry 12 in the translator's notes asks what happens to the series whose terms are (n cubed + 1) over (n to the fifth + n) as n grows.

options.text: The terms behave like 1 over n squared, since the leading powers give n cubed over n to the fifth.
The terms behave like 1 over n cubed, since the larger denominator power wins, and the series diverges.
options.misconception: picks the wrong leading power of the denominator

options.text: The terms behave like n squared, since dividing by a higher power of n makes the ratio grow.
options.misconception: divides the leading powers the wrong way round

options.text: The terms behave like 1 over n, since the sum of the powers n cubed and n to the fifth is n to the eighth.
options.misconception: adds the exponents instead of subtracting them

questions.explanation: The leading power of the numerator is the third and of the denominator the fifth, so the terms behave like 1 over n squared. A p-series with p = 2 converges, and the smaller terms do not change that.
questions.hint: Subtract the leading powers of numerator and denominator.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: The limit comparison test
questions.learningObjective: Compute the limit of a quotient of matching terms.
questions.stem: Note 27 of the translator's log asks for the value of the limit of a_n over b_n when a_n = n over (n squared + 1) and b_n = 1 over n.
questions.explanation: The quotient is n squared over (n squared + 1), which tends to 1. A finite positive limit of 1 means the two series have the same convergence behaviour.
questions.hint: Form the quotient and take its limit.

questions.topic: Direct comparison with a geometric series

questions.stem: A footnote in the translation explains why the series with terms 1 over n factorial can be handled by comparing each term with a geometric term.

options.text: Because 1 over n factorial is larger than the matching geometric term for every n.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the comparison

options.text: Because 1 over n factorial never exceeds 1 over 2 to the power n minus 1, and that geometric series converges.
Because the factorial in the denominator gives a constant ratio.
options.misconception: believes factorial terms have a constant ratio

options.text: Because the factorial in the denominator makes the terms grow, so the series diverges by comparison.
options.misconception: thinks a growing denominator makes terms grow

questions.explanation: For every n at least 1 the factorial is at least 2 to the power n minus 1, so the terms of the factorial series are bounded above by the terms of a convergent geometric series.
questions.hint: Compare factorials with powers of two.

options.text: The two columns track each other because the series and the integral are the same object in two disguises.
options.misconception: believes the series and the integral coincide exactly

options.text: The two columns track each other because the integral test guarantees equality of the two values.
options.misconception: reads the integral test as an equality claim

options.text: The two columns track each other because the terms decrease slowly enough for the sum to grow without bound.
options.misconception: ignores the test hypothesis that f must decrease

options.text: The two columns track each other because a positive decreasing function gives comparable sums and integrals.

options.text: The series converges exactly when the corresponding improper integral diverges to plus infinity.

options.text: The series converges exactly when the corresponding improper integral is finite but not computable.

The series and the integral always differ by exactly the first term of the series.
options.misconception: believes the gap is always the first term

questions.explanation: The integral test says that for a positive continuous decreasing function the series and the improper integral converge or diverge together.

options.text: The rule is false, because termwise comparison says nothing about the behaviour of the partial sums.
options.misconception: believes termwise comparison is powerless

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: Comparing a series with an improper integral
questions.learningObjective: Read the value of an improper integral from tabulated values.
questions.stem: A translator's sheet records the values of the integral of 1 over x to the fourth from 1 to N as 0, 0.2917, 0.3210, 0.3281 and 0.3307 for N equal to 1 to 5.

options.text: The values level off towards one third, so the series with the matching terms must have a sum of one third.
options.misconception: confuses the integral limit with the series sum

options.text: The values level off towards one third, which is the value of the improper integral from 1 to infinity.
The values keep climbing without a ceiling, so the improper integral diverges.
options.misconception: reads a rising list as divergence

options.text: The values are exactly the partial sums of the matching series, so the two are identical.
options.misconception: claims the tabulated values are series partial sums

questions.explanation: The tabulated values are 1 over 3 minus 1 over 3N cubed, which climb towards one third, and that is the value of the improper integral.
questions.hint: Look for the pattern in the tabulated values.
